boards.title: Only Happens Here: 10 Traditions That Make No Sense Anywhere Else
boards.description: Ten college-specific ceremonies, objects, songs, and symbols documented by Trinity College.

cards.title: Sign the Charter and Standing Rules
cards.subtitle: President’s Convocation, Trinity Chapel
cards.notes: At Convocation, watch incoming students complete Trinity’s symbolic enrollment by signing the Charter and Standing Rules in the Chapel.
cards.short_summary: Trinity’s oldest continuously observed tradition marks the academic year’s opening.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity identifies matriculation as its oldest continuously observed tradition; incoming first-years sign the Charter and Standing Rules during the Chapel ceremony.
cards.access_notes: This is part of the President’s Convocation for incoming students; consult the College’s Convocation information for the current program.

cards.title: Notice the Dark Blue and Gold
cards.subtitle: College-wide colors
cards.notes: Use the official dark blue and gold as a visual thread when documenting campus ceremonies, athletic settings, or archival Trinity imagery.
cards.short_summary: Students selected the colors after Trinity moved to its current campus in 1878.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity states that students voted for dark blue and gold as the colors for the “new Trinity” after the 1878 move.
cards.access_notes: A campus identity tradition rather than a scheduled public activity.

cards.title: Read the Seal’s 1845 Story
cards.subtitle: College seal and ceremonial imagery
cards.notes: Look closely at the seal in official settings and compare its Episcopal imagery, Seabury Hall façade, and thirteen-star reference.
cards.short_summary: The seal dates to the College’s 1845 name change from Washington College.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity dates its seal to 1845 and explains that its design reflects Episcopal roots, Seabury Hall, and thirteen colonies.
cards.access_notes: A ceremonial and institutional symbol; view it in official College materials and settings.

cards.title: See the Convocation Lemon Squeeze
cards.subtitle: President’s Convocation
cards.notes: If attending Convocation, look for the president’s ceremonial squeeze of a fresh lemon and the lemonade that follows for the incoming class.
cards.short_summary: A wooden squeezer became a class-rivalry object before its present Convocation role.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity says the current lemon squeezer appears only at Convocation, when the president squeezes a lemon for a toast to the incoming class.
cards.access_notes: Part of Convocation programming; availability depends on the College’s current event schedule.

cards.title: Listen for ’Neath the Elms
cards.subtitle: Trinity Pipes and campus ceremonies
cards.notes: Listen for “’Neath the Elms” at a Trinity musical or ceremonial occasion, and connect the performance to the College’s a cappella history.
cards.short_summary: The song was written in 1882 by student Augustus P. Burgwin and is sung by the Trinity Pipes.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity documents “’Neath the Elms” as an 1882 student-written alma mater song sung by the Trinity Pipes.
cards.access_notes: Performance opportunities vary; check current College music and event listings.

cards.title: Respect the Commencement Stone
cards.subtitle: Fuller Arch at Northam Towers, Long Walk
cards.notes: Find the rectangular inscription stone by Fuller Arch; observe it from the sidewalk and leave its senior-only ceremonial step to Commencement.
cards.short_summary: Students traditionally avoid the stone before graduation, then seniors step on it at Commencement.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity documents the tradition of avoiding the Long Walk inscription before Commencement and seniors ceremonially stepping on it when graduating.
cards.access_notes: Outdoor campus feature; respect ceremonies, pedestrian access, and College guidance.

cards.title: Meet the Unabashed Bantam
cards.subtitle: Trinity athletics and campus identity
cards.notes: Spot the Bantam in official athletic or campus settings and trace the mascot back to the 1899 alumni-dinner speech that named it.
cards.short_summary: The mascot grew from an 1899 comparison of Trinity to a proud, self-possessed rooster.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity traces the Bantam name to Joseph Buffington’s 1899 speech and says students, alumni, and press adopted it for Trinity teams.
cards.access_notes: A College mascot and athletics tradition; event access varies by venue and schedule.

cards.title: Follow the Hat’s Handoff
cards.subtitle: Half-Century event and alumni parade
cards.notes: At Reunion, watch for the previous 50th class to pass its hat forward; each newly inducted class adds a Trinity-experience pin.
cards.short_summary: The receiving class president wears the evolving hat in Saturday’s alumni parade.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity says the prior 50th reunion class passes the hat at the Half-Century event, and the new class adds a representative pin.
cards.access_notes: Reunion programming is event-specific; consult current alumni and family event information.

cards.title: Watch for the Mace in Procession
cards.subtitle: Academic processions
cards.notes: During an academic procession, look for the 44-inch Morgan Mace preceding the president and note its six institutional seals.
cards.short_summary: Presented in 1950, the mace represents the president’s executive authority.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity states that the Owen Morgan Mace precedes the president in academic processions and symbolizes executive power.
cards.access_notes: Visible during applicable College academic ceremonies; timing depends on the current ceremony program.

cards.title: Notice the Book at Commencement
cards.subtitle: Trinity Commencement
cards.notes: At Commencement, notice the Book placed in each graduate’s hands, a practice Trinity says began accidentally at its first commencement.
cards.short_summary: The Book tradition dates to 1827, when President Brownell used the bound order of exercises.
cards.evidence_claim: Trinity says the Book has been placed in every graduate’s hands since the College’s first commencement in 1827.
cards.access_notes: Part of Commencement; attendance and viewing arrangements are set by the College for each ceremony.
